questions.q: A bond has a 6% coupon but the market yield to maturity is 8%. What should you expect about its price relative to face value?
options: It should trade above face value (at a premium)
It should trade exactly at face value
It should trade below face value (at a discount)
Price and coupon rate are unrelated, so nothing can be inferred
questions.explain: When the coupon rate is below the market yield, the bond must trade at a discount to face value so the buyer still earns the going market rate overall.

options: The bond's coupon rate expressed in years
The weighted-average time until the bond's cash flows are received, weighted by each cash flow's present value
The exact number of years until the bond matures
The bond's credit rating relative to Treasuries
questions.explain: Macaulay duration weights the timing of each cash flow by its share of the bond's present value, producing a weighted-average time to receipt that is typically less than the bond's maturity.

questions.q: A bond has a modified duration of 2.62. If yields rise by 1 percentage point, what is the approximate expected price change?
options: The price rises by about 2.62%
The price falls by about 2.62%
The price is unaffected by yield changes
The price falls by exactly 2.62 dollars regardless of the bond's price
questions.explain: Modified duration approximates the percentage price change for a 1-percentage-point yield change; a rise in yield produces an approximate fall in price of that percentage.

questions.q: Why is duration alone not a complete measure of a bond's interest-rate sensitivity?
options: Duration ignores the bond's face value entirely
Duration is a linear approximation, but the real price-yield relationship is curved (convex), which duration alone misses
Duration only applies to bonds with zero coupons
Duration changes the bond's credit rating
questions.explain: Duration assumes price moves proportionally with yield (a straight line), but the actual relationship curves. Convexity captures that curvature as a correction term.

questions.q: In the approximation ΔP/P ≈ −D×Δy + ½×C×(Δy)², why does the convexity term benefit a bondholder in both directions (yields rising or falling)?
options: Because convexity is always negative for a plain bond
Because the convexity term is squared, making it always non-negative, slightly cushioning losses when yields rise and boosting gains when yields fall
Because convexity only matters when yields fall, never when they rise
Because convexity replaces duration entirely in the formula
questions.explain: Since (Δy)² is always non-negative, the convexity term adds a small positive adjustment regardless of whether yields rise or fall — cushioning losses on the way up and adding extra gains on the way down.
